```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
set.seed(2026)
# non-ASCII characters in output and plots under a "C" locale
invisible(Sys.setlocale("LC_CTYPE", "C.UTF-8"))
fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
pct <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(fmt(100 * x, d), "%")
```

A rapid test, a spam filter, an algorithm that predicts whether a student will pass: they all give a **binary prediction**, "positive" or "negative". How good is such a prediction? The answer is not one number but several, and each answers a different question. All of them are [conditional probabilities](../conditional-probability/index.qmd).

## The confusion matrix

We compare prediction and reality in $\Sigma$ cases and record the results in a **confusion matrix**:

| Actual condition | Predicted negative | Predicted positive | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Negative** | $\alpha$ (true negatives) | $\beta$ (false positives) | $O_1 = \alpha + \beta$ |
| **Positive** | $\gamma$ (false negatives) | $\delta$ (true positives) | $O_2 = \gamma + \delta$ |
| **Total** | $P_1 = \alpha + \gamma$ | $P_2 = \beta + \delta$ | $\Sigma$ |

From it we define:

- **Accuracy** (PAC, percentage accuracy in classification): $(\alpha + \delta)/\Sigma$, the share of correct predictions.
- **Sensitivity** (TPR): $\delta / O_2$, of those who **are** positive, how many the test detects.
- **Specificity** (TNR): $\alpha / O_1$, of those who **are** negative, how many it recognises as negative.
- **Positive predictive value** (PPV): $\delta / P_2$, of those who **tested** positive, how many really are positive.
- **Negative predictive value** (NPV): $\alpha / P_1$, of those who **tested** negative, how many really are negative.

Sensitivity and specificity are read **along the rows**: they start from the actual condition. PPV and NPV are read **down the columns**: they start from the test result, which is what the doctor or the patient sees.

## A real example

A study compared the ID NOW rapid test with the molecular RT-PCR test in 974 people ([eLife, 2021](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.65726)). Of the 785 symptomatic patients, 21 were positive on both tests and 2 only on RT-PCR. All 189 asymptomatic patients were negative on both. Taking RT-PCR as the actual condition:

| RT-PCR | ID NOW negative | ID NOW positive | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Negative** | 951 | 0 | 951 |
| **Positive** | 2 | 21 | 23 |
| **Total** | 953 | 21 | 974 |

```{r}
#| label: id-now
metrics <- function(a, b, g, d) {
  c(PAC = (a + d) / (a + b + g + d), sensitivity = d / (g + d), specificity = a / (a + b),
    PPV = d / (b + d), NPV = a / (a + g))
}
round(metrics(a = 951, b = 0, g = 2, d = 21), 3)
```

Specificity and PPV are 100%: no false positives. Sensitivity is `r pct(21/23)`: the test missed 2 of the 23 positives.

//| echo: false
viewof preset27 = Inputs.select(new Map([

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof cm27 = Inputs.form({
  a: Inputs.number([0, 1e6], {label: "α: true negatives", step: 1, value: preset27[0]}),
  b: Inputs.number([0, 1e6], {label: "β: false positives", step: 1, value: preset27[1]}),
  g: Inputs.number([0, 1e6], {label: "γ: false negatives", step: 1, value: preset27[2]}),
  d: Inputs.number([0, 1e6], {label: "δ: true positives", step: 1, value: preset27[3]})
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const {a, b, g, d} = cm27, S = a + b + g + d;
  if (!(S > 0)) return html`<div class="ix-note">Enter positive numbers.</div>`;
  const O1 = a + b, O2 = g + d, P1 = a + g, P2 = b + d;
  const W = 340, H = 220, m = 20, w1 = O1 / S * W;
  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${W + 2 * m} ${H + 2 * m + 10}`).style("width", "100%").style("max-width", "380px").style("font", "12px sans-serif");
  const cell = (x, y, w, h, fill, lab) => { if (w <= 0 || h <= 0) return; svg.append("rect").attr("x", m + x).attr("y", m + y).attr("width", w).attr("height", h).attr("fill", fill).attr("stroke", "#fff").attr("stroke-width", 2); if (w > 26 && h > 16) svg.append("text").attr("x", m + x + w / 2).attr("y", m + y + h / 2).attr("dy", "0.35em").attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("fill", "#fff").attr("font-weight", "bold").text(lab); };
  const hb = O1 ? b / O1 * H : 0, hd = O2 ? d / O2 * H : 0;
  cell(0, 0, w1, hb, "#c62828", "β");
  cell(0, hb, w1, H - hb, "#4e79a7", "α");
  cell(w1, 0, W - w1, hd, "#59a14f", "δ");
  cell(w1, hd, W - w1, H - hd, "#f28e2b", "γ");
  svg.append("text").attr("x", m + w1 / 2).attr("y", H + 2 * m).attr("text-anchor", "middle").text("Negative");
  svg.append("text").attr("x", m + w1 + (W - w1) / 2).attr("y", H + 2 * m).attr("text-anchor", "middle").text("Positive");
  const f = (x, y) => y ? `${x.toLocaleString("en-GB")}/${y.toLocaleString("en-GB")} = ${(x / y).toLocaleString("en-GB", {style: "percent", maximumFractionDigits: 1})}` : "undefined";
  return html`<div class="ix-row"><div style="flex:0 1 380px">${svg.node()}
    <div class="ix-note">Blue: true negatives. Red: false positives. Orange: false negatives. Green: true positives.</div></div><div>
    <table class="ix-tbl">
      <tr><td>PAC</td><td><b>${f(a + d, S)}</b></td></tr>
      <tr><td>Sensitivity δ/O₂</td><td><b>${f(d, O2)}</b></td></tr>
      <tr><td>Specificity α/O₁</td><td><b>${f(a, O1)}</b></td></tr>
      <tr><td>PPV δ/P₂</td><td><b>${f(d, P2)}</b></td></tr>
      <tr><td>NPV α/P₁</td><td><b>${f(a, P1)}</b></td></tr>
    </table></div></div>`;
}
```
:::

Pick the "test" that always says negative: its accuracy is 95%, yet it detects **no** positive case. When one class is rare, accuracy alone is misleading. That is why we need sensitivity and specificity.

## The measures as conditional probabilities

Let $A$ = {the prediction is positive} and $B$ = {the actual condition is positive}. In the table, $N(B) = O_2$, $N(A) = P_2$, $N(A \cap B) = \delta$ and $N(A' \cap B') = \alpha$. Hence:

| Measure | Conditional probability | Also called |
|---|---|---|
| Sensitivity | $P(A \mid B)$ | true positive rate (TPR), recall |
| $1 -$ sensitivity | $P(A' \mid B)$ | false negative rate (FNR) |
| Specificity | $P(A' \mid B')$ | true negative rate (TNR) |
| $1 -$ specificity | $P(A \mid B')$ | false positive rate (FPR) |
| PPV | $P(B \mid A)$ | precision |
| NPV | $P(B' \mid A')$ | |

Sensitivity and PPV are the two directions of the same conditioning: $P(A \mid B)$ and $P(B \mid A)$. As we saw with [Bayes' theorem](../bayes-theorem/index.qmd), getting from one to the other also requires $P(B)$, how common the condition is in the population. That is the subject of the next post.

The measures are not only for medical tests but for any "symptom" $A$ linked to a "condition" $B$. If, for example, 90% of people with lung cancer and 30% of people without it are smokers, then smoking as a "test" for the disease has sensitivity $P(A \mid B) = 0.9$ and specificity $P(A' \mid B') = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7$.

## Key takeaways

- The **confusion matrix** compares prediction and reality: true/false positives and negatives.
- **Sensitivity** $= P(\text{positive test} \mid \text{positive})$ and **specificity** $= P(\text{negative test} \mid \text{negative})$: properties of the test.
- **PPV** $= P(\text{positive} \mid \text{positive test})$ and **NPV** $= P(\text{negative} \mid \text{negative test})$: what matters to whoever sees the result.
- **Accuracy** is misleading when one class is rare.

## Review questions

**1. Quick quiz.**

::: {.ix-panel}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
quiz27 = [
  {q: "A test is positive in 95% of people who have the disease. Which measure is this?",
   opts: ["Specificity", "Sensitivity", "PPV", "NPV"], ans: 1,
   why: "We start from those who have the disease (a row of the table): P(positive test | disease) = sensitivity."},
  {q: "Of those who tested positive, 40% really have the disease. Which measure is this?",
   opts: ["Sensitivity", "PPV", "Specificity", "Accuracy"], ans: 1,
   why: "We start from the test result (a column of the table): P(disease | positive test) = PPV."},
  {q: "In a town of 1,000 people, 10% have a disease. A test has sensitivity 80% and specificity 70%. How many patients will be missed?",
   opts: ["20", "80", "270", "30"], ans: 0,
   why: "There are 100 patients. The test detects 80% of them, 80 people, and misses 20 (false negatives)."},
  {q: "Which measure equals 1 − specificity?",
   opts: ["False negative rate", "False positive rate", "NPV", "1 − PPV"], ans: 1,
   why: "1 − P(negative | negative condition) = P(positive | negative condition), the false positive rate among negatives."}
]
{
  const root = html`<div></div>`, score = html`<div class="ix-note"></div>`, done = new Map();
  quiz27.forEach((item, k) => {
    const fb = html`<div class="ix-note"></div>`;
    const btns = item.opts.map(o => html`<button>${o}</button>`);
    const opts = html`<div style="margin:4px 0 0 6px">${btns.map((b, j) => {
      b.onclick = () => {
        const ok = j === item.ans; done.set(k, ok);
        btns.forEach(x => x.className = "");
        b.className = ok ? "ix-picked-ok" : "ix-picked-no";
        fb.innerHTML = (ok ? `<span class="ix-ok">✓ Correct.</span> ` : `<span class="ix-no">✗ Not quite.</span> `) + item.why;
        score.innerHTML = `<b>Correct: ${[...done.values()].filter(x => x).length} of ${quiz27.length}</b>`;
      };
      return b;
    })}</div>`;
    root.append(html`<div style="margin:12px 0"><div>${k + 1}. ${item.q}</div>${opts}${fb}</div>`);
  });
  root.append(score);
  return root;
}
```
:::

**2.** Another study ([Jegerlehner et al., IJID, 2021](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijid.2021.07.010)) tested 1,465 people. RT-PCR was positive in 141. The rapid antigen test was positive in 94 people and negative or invalid in the remaining 1,371. Its sensitivity was 65.3% and its specificity 99.9%. (a) Fill in the confusion matrix. (b) Compute accuracy, PPV and NPV.

**3.** A "test" returns a positive result at random, with probability 50%, regardless of the actual condition. What are its sensitivity and specificity?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

2. (a) True positives: $0.653 \cdot 141 \approx 92$, so false negatives $141 - 92 = 49$. False positives: $94 - 92 = 2$. RT-PCR negatives: $1{,}465 - 141 = 1{,}324$, so true negatives $1{,}324 - 2 = 1{,}322$ (specificity $1{,}322/1{,}324 \approx 99.85\%$). (b) Accuracy $= (1{,}322 + 92)/1{,}465 \approx 96.5\%$, PPV $= 92/94 \approx 97.9\%$, NPV $= 1{,}322/1{,}371 \approx 96.4\%$. Check them in the calculator.
3. Sensitivity 50% and specificity 50%: the test tells nothing apart. We will meet it again on the ROC curve, where such tests lie on the diagonal.
:::
